pairs.rationale: Mark introduces Jesus Christ as Son of God; John's written-purpose statement likewise joins Jesus, the Christ and the Son of God. John explains believing and life in His name, while Mark's verse introduces the gospel rather than stating that whole purpose.

The announced messenger preparing the way corresponds to Malachi's messenger clause. Mark introduces the combined citation under Isaiah's name; the following wilderness-voice verse corresponds to Isaiah 40:3. Malachi's supplied wording has the way before My face, while Mark has Thy face and Thy way; the attribution and wording are preserved rather than silently corrected.

The phrase about sending a messenger before Thy face also recalls Exodus' I send My angel before your face. Exodus concerns guidance into a prepared land; Mark uses the preparatory message in its opening about John. The shared sending formula does not identify John as the angel in Exodus.

Mark's wilderness voice and commands to prepare the Lord's way and straighten His paths quote the Isaiah passage named in the preceding introduction. Isaiah's supplied final phrase is the paths of our God.

Both locate John in the wilderness and describe a baptism of repentance for forgiveness of sins. Luke introduces God's word coming to John and then names the Jordan region; Mark summarizes John's appearing and proclamation.
Both describe people from Jerusalem and Judea going to John and receiving baptism in the Jordan while confessing sins. Matthew also names the surrounding Jordan region.
Both describe John's camel-hair clothing, leather belt and food of locusts and wild honey.
Both record John's announcement of a stronger coming One and his unworthiness to untie that One's sandal strap. Mark adds stooping, while Luke includes the baptism contrast within the same verse.
Both contrast John's water baptism with the coming One's baptism in the Holy Spirit. Luke adds fire; Mark's cited source verse does not contain that word.
Both bring Jesus from Galilee to John at the Jordan for baptism. Mark specifies Nazareth and states that He was baptized; Matthew's verse narrates His arrival with the purpose of being baptized.

Both describe Jesus emerging from the water, an opening of heaven and the Spirit descending like a dove. Mark says heaven was torn open and the Spirit descended into Him, while Matthew says the heavens opened and the Spirit came upon Him in this edition.
Both record the heavenly declaration of Jesus as beloved Son and of divine pleasure in Him. Mark gives direct address, Thou art, while Matthew gives This is; the grammatical difference is retained.

Both connect the Spirit with Jesus' movement into the wilderness for testing. Mark says the Spirit drove Him, while Matthew says He was led; Matthew names the devil in this verse and Mark names Satan in the following verse.

Both place Jesus' testing in the wilderness in a forty-day setting. Matthew explicitly describes fasting forty days and nights; Mark says He was there forty days being tempted by Satan. These verses do not supply Mark's wild animals or angelic ministry.

Both wilderness accounts describe angels ministering to Jesus. Matthew places their arrival after the devil leaves; Mark includes the ministry in a compressed description of the wilderness stay without that explicit timing.
Both relate Jesus' arrival or withdrawal into Galilee to John having been handed over. Matthew says Jesus heard of it and withdrew; Mark additionally introduces His proclamation of God's gospel.

Both summarize Jesus' proclamation through the kingdom's nearness and the call to repent. Mark additionally names fulfillment of the appointed time and belief in the gospel; Matthew says kingdom of the heavens.
Both describe Jesus seeing the brothers Simon and Andrew casting a net beside the Sea of Galilee and identify them as fishermen. Matthew adds that Simon is called Peter.
Both call the fishermen to come after Jesus with the promise of making them fishers of people or men. Mark's wording includes become.
Both describe the immediate response of leaving the nets and following Jesus.
Both describe Jesus seeing James and John, Zebedee's sons, in the boat tending their nets. Matthew explicitly places Zebedee with them and includes Jesus' call within this verse.
Both narrate the call of Zebedee's sons and their leaving the boat and father to follow. Mark also mentions hired workers in the boat; Matthew does not supply that detail.
Both place Jesus' teaching in Capernaum on the Sabbath. Mark explicitly names the synagogue here, while Luke's following narrative supplies the synagogue setting.
Both describe astonishment at Jesus' teaching because it has authority. Mark adds the contrast with the scribes, which Luke's cited verse does not repeat.
Both introduce a man with an unclean spirit in the synagogue who cries out. Luke calls it the spirit of an unclean demon and specifies a loud voice.
Both cries address Jesus of Nazareth, ask whether He has come to destroy them and identify Him as God's Holy One. Luke adds the opening Ah.
Both give Jesus' rebuke commanding silence and departure from the man. Mark says Be muzzled, while Luke says Be silent in the supplied wording.

Both narrate the spirit's departure with a violent bodily movement. Mark describes convulsing and a loud cry; Luke describes the man being thrown down and expressly says he was not harmed. The movement descriptions are not treated as identical.
Both depict amazement and discussion of Jesus' authority to command unclean spirits. Mark calls it new teaching and says the spirits obey; Luke names authority and power and says they come out.
Both conclude the synagogue exorcism with the report about Jesus spreading throughout the surrounding region. Mark explicitly names Galilee.
Both move from the synagogue into Simon's house. Mark adds Andrew and the accompanying James and John; Luke includes the mother-in-law's fever and request for help within the same verse.
Both describe Simon Peter's mother-in-law lying ill with fever. Matthew places Jesus' seeing her in Peter's house; Mark adds that they immediately told Him about her.
Both connect Jesus' contact with her hand to the fever's departure, her rising and her service. Mark says she served them and Matthew says Him.

Both describe people bringing the sick at sunset and healing accompanied by expulsions of demons. Luke additionally gives laying hands on each sick person and the demons' cries; Mark's source verse introduces the brought groups.

Both describe healings, expulsions and Jesus preventing demons from speaking because they know Him. Mark says He healed many; Luke says He healed each person brought and explicitly reports the demons identifying Him as God's Son and the Christ.

Both describe Jesus withdrawing to deserted places for prayer. Mark narrates a particular predawn departure, while Luke describes His repeated practice without that time notice; this is a shared practice rather than an identification of one occasion.
Both describe people seeking Jesus after His withdrawal to a deserted place. Mark names Simon and his companions; Luke names the crowds, so the seeking groups are not silently equated.

Both describe the searchers reaching Jesus after His withdrawal. Mark records the companions' statement that everyone is seeking Him; Luke reports the crowds trying to prevent His departure without reproducing that statement.

Both give Jesus' purpose of proclaiming in other towns or cities as His reason to move on. Mark says for this He came out; Luke explicitly names the good news of God's kingdom and says for this He was sent.

Both summarize a Galilean circuit of proclamation in synagogues. Mark explicitly names casting out demons; Matthew adds teaching and healing every disease and infirmity. The summaries share the region and activity without being identical in scope.
Both narrate a leper approaching Jesus and saying that Jesus can cleanse him if willing. Mark describes pleading and kneeling; Matthew describes bowing and addresses Him as Lord.

Both describe Jesus reaching out, touching the man and declaring His willingness with the command to be cleansed. Mark explicitly gives compassion; Matthew's verse also reports the immediate cleansing.
Both state the immediate cleansing of leprosy. Matthew joins it to Jesus' touch and command within the same verse.

Mark's stern warning and immediate dismissal introduce the instruction in its following verse; Matthew directly records a warning to tell no one and a command to go to the priest. Matthew does not separately describe the forceful immediate dismissal.
Both prohibit telling others and direct the healed man to show himself to the priest and make Moses' prescribed offering as testimony. Mark explicitly calls it the offering for cleansing.

Both link the spreading report with crowds seeking Jesus and His remaining or withdrawing in deserted places. Mark specifically attributes publicity to the healed man and says Jesus could not enter a city openly; Luke does not supply those exact causal details and adds prayer.

Both introduce the paralytic-healing episode with Jesus returning to His own or home city. Mark explicitly names Capernaum and an interval of days; Matthew says His own city after a boat crossing without those details in its verse.

Both place Jesus teaching amid a gathering that prevents access for the paralytic's bearers. Mark describes the crowded house and doorway; Luke names the seated legal teachers and describes the crowd preventing entry before the lowering through the roof.
Both describe men carrying a paralyzed man on a bed in order to place him before Jesus. Mark specifies four bearers; Luke does not give their number.

Both have the bearers overcome crowd-blocked access by lowering the paralytic and his bed through the roof. Mark describes removing and digging through the roof, while Luke says through the tiles; the construction descriptions remain distinct.
Both have Jesus see their faith and pronounce the paralytic's sins forgiven. Mark addresses him as Child, while Luke's supplied address is Man.
Both describe scribes reasoning inwardly about the forgiveness declaration. Luke also names Pharisees and includes the blasphemy objection in the same verse.
Both record the objection that Jesus' words are blasphemous and that only God can forgive sins. Luke explicitly places the question in the legal teachers' reasoning.
Both have Jesus perceive the hearers' reasoning and ask why they reason this way in their hearts. Mark adds that He knew in His spirit.
Both ask which is easier, saying sins are forgiven or commanding the paralytic to rise and walk. Mark includes taking the mat in the second alternative.

Both explain the healing command through the Son of Man's authority on earth to forgive sins and turn to address the paralytic. Matthew includes the ensuing command within the same verse; Mark gives it in the next verse.
Both command the paralyzed man to rise, take his bed and go home. Luke includes the preceding statement about the Son of Man's authority within the same verse.

Both narrate the man rising, taking what he had been lying on, and departing, with witnesses amazed and glorifying God. Luke explicitly says he went home; Mark says he went out before everyone. Mark says the witnesses had never seen anything like it; Luke calls it extraordinary and explicitly describes fear.
Both call the tax collector Levi from the tax station with Follow Me and describe his rising to follow. Mark names him son of Alphaeus; Luke adds leaving everything and does not give that patronymic.

Both depict Jesus at a meal with many tax collectors and others. Luke explicitly calls it Levi's great feast in his house, while Mark uses his house and calls the other diners sinners. Those wording differences are retained.

Both have Pharisees and scribes object to the disciples about eating with tax collectors and sinners. Mark asks why He eats; Luke's question is why you eat and drink, so the grammatical subjects and added drinking are not made identical.
Both answer through the healthy-and-sick physician analogy and Jesus' mission to call sinners rather than the righteous. Luke adds to repentance, which Mark's supplied verse does not include.

Both contrast John's disciples and the Pharisees fasting with Jesus' disciples not fasting. Matthew identifies John's disciples as the questioners and says often; Mark introduces the fasting situation and reports those approaching with the question.

Both explain the wedding companions' behavior by the bridegroom's presence. Mark asks whether they can fast, while Matthew asks whether they can mourn; the actions are related within the fasting dispute but the words differ.
Both predict that when the bridegroom is taken away the companions will fast. Mark adds on that day, while Matthew includes the preceding presence contrast within the same verse.
Both describe an unshrunk patch pulling away from an old garment and producing a worse tear as the illustration following the fasting question.
Both warn that new wine in old wineskins bursts the skins and loses wine and skins, then require fresh skins. Matthew explicitly adds that both are preserved.
Both have Jesus pass through grainfields on a Sabbath while His disciples pluck heads of grain. Matthew explicitly mentions their hunger and eating; Mark's source verse does not state those details.
Both have Pharisees challenge Jesus about the disciples' doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath in the grainfields.
Both answer by asking whether the opponents have read what David and his companions did when hungry. Mark additionally says David was in need.

Both recall David entering God's house, eating the holy presentation bread restricted to priests and sharing in the event with his companions. Mark names Abiathar as high priest; Matthew's cited verse gives no priestly name, so the name is not imported into it.

Samuel supplies the episode of David requesting and receiving holy presentation loaves, with discussion about the accompanying young men's purity. Saints Samuel names the priest Abimelech, whereas Mark names Abiathar as high priest. The cross-reference preserves both names and does not equate the two priestly references or treat Samuel as repeating Mark's full legal formulation.

Deuteronomy grounds the Sabbath in rest extending to servants and in remembrance of release from slavery; Mark states that the Sabbath was made for the human being rather than the reverse. This is a concrete comparison of the Sabbath's human benefit, not a claim that Deuteronomy quotes Mark's maxim.
Both conclude the grainfield dispute with the Son of Man's lordship over the Sabbath. Mark's wording includes even.

deferred.reason: The whole city's gathering at the door was read in the evening-healing context. The corresponding healing accounts do not reproduce this precise collective doorway notice; generic crowd gatherings were not retained merely to complete this unit.

The seaside departure, whole crowd and teaching notice before Levi's call were read. The parallel call accounts do not reproduce that complete transitional scene, and generic seaside or teaching notices were not used to manufacture a retained pair.

review_notes: Read all 73 actual source units in Mark 1–2 from the exact pinned Saints English record, after the parent confirmed that every original Matthew source unit had been read.

Every retained target was read in the exact Saints originals with the surrounding narrative or discourse where needed. Original target ordering, absent-verse gaps and Greek-based book divisions remain intact.

The opening composite citation is handled without silently changing Mark's Isaiah attribution: the messenger clause is compared with Malachi 3:1 and Exodus 23:20, and the wilderness-voice clause with Isaiah 40:3.

Mark's Spirit descending into Him and Matthew's upon Him are kept distinct. Luke's fire in John's baptism saying is not added to Mark, and Mark's wild animals are not inserted into the other wilderness accounts.

The searching groups in Mark and Luke, the healing-summary quantities, the Levi call details, pronouns in the meal complaint and the tile-versus-dug-roof descriptions are qualified rather than harmonized.

The bread episode preserves Mark's Abiathar and the Saints Samuel record's Abimelech, without declaring the priest names identical or importing a different patronymic. Saints 1 Samuel 21:2–7 is used as saved.

A target range counts as one pair. Three sources have additional independently useful targets: Mark 1:2 for the composite wording, Mark 1:13 for angelic ministry alongside the testing setting, and Mark 2:26 for the original bread episode beside the Gospel parallel. Completion still counts each source only once.
The two deferred units receive zero completion credit. The hourly numerical target does not justify a generic connection.
No source wording, display wording, continuations, verse IDs or division membership is edited. This is an AI-assisted English initial passage review, with independent specialist review pending.
